name: CANDLE syndrome
aliases: chronic atypical neutrophilic dermatosis with lipodystrophy and elevated temperature

reference.source: Textbook of Autoinflammation / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A type I interferonopathy caused by mutations affecting the proteasome, classically PSMB8, impairing protein degradation
Presents in infancy or early childhood with recurrent fevers, violaceous annular skin plaques, and progressive lipodystrophy
Facial and limb fat loss produces a characteristic pinched appearance, while periorbital oedema and swelling are common
Additional features include arthralgia, hepatosplenomegaly, growth impairment, and delayed physical development
A raised interferon signature in blood is a key laboratory clue supporting an interferonopathy
Skin biopsy shows an atypical mononuclear and neutrophilic dermal infiltrate rather than a simple neutrophilic dermatosis
Janus kinase (JAK) inhibition targets the interferon pathway and can improve systemic and cutaneous features, though damage may be only partly reversible
reference.pathophysiology: CANDLE syndrome is a proteasome-associated autoinflammatory disease, most often from mutations in PSMB8 and related proteasome or immunoproteasome subunit genes. Defective proteasome function impairs clearance of ubiquitinated and oxidised proteins, causing cellular stress that triggers excessive type I interferon production. This interferon-dominated inflammation drives recurrent fevers, an atypical neutrophilic dermatosis, panniculitis with resulting lipodystrophy, and multi-organ involvement. The prominent interferon signature explains both the clinical phenotype and the rationale for JAK inhibition, which dampens interferon signalling.
additionalDifferentials: SAVI and other type I interferonopathies
Sweet syndrome and other neutrophilic dermatoses
additionalInvestigations: Genetic testing for PSMB8 and other proteasome subunit gene mutations
Interferon signature (interferon-stimulated gene expression) in blood
Skin biopsy demonstrating atypical mixed dermal infiltrate and panniculitis
Acute-phase reactants and full blood count
Assessment of metabolic and lipid profile given lipodystrophy
Imaging and growth monitoring for organomegaly and developmental delay
redFlags: Progressive organ dysfunction from sustained interferon-driven inflammation
Severe growth failure and developmental delay
Refractory systemic inflammation despite conventional immunosuppression
reference.prognosis: CANDLE is a chronic progressive disease; JAK inhibition can substantially reduce inflammation and improve quality of life, but established lipodystrophy and organ damage may persist.
pitfalls: Attributing early features to juvenile dermatomyositis or systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and missing the interferonopathy
Failing to request an interferon signature when standard autoimmune workup is inconclusive
Expecting full reversal of lipodystrophy with treatment
Relying on conventional immunosuppression that inadequately targets interferon signalling
management: Use a JAK inhibitor such as baricitinib or ruxolitinib as the mainstay to suppress the type I interferon-driven inflammation
Add corticosteroids for partial control, recognising that conventional immunosuppressants are often ineffective
Monitor for infection during JAK inhibition, together with growth, blood counts and lipid and metabolic parameters
Manage established lipodystrophy and its metabolic consequences with dietetic and endocrine input
Track disease activity using the blood interferon signature and acute-phase reactants
Offer genetic testing and counselling for the underlying PSMB8 and related proteasome-gene mutations
Coordinate care across clinical immunology, rheumatology and dermatology
